llama.types: Andean herders and researchers separate two main llama fleece types. The ccara or q'ara llama is double-coated, with more guard hair and less undercoat, while the ch'aku or th'ampulli type is woolly, single-coated and heavier-fleeced. A study of a llama population in southern Bolivia reported th'ampulli fleeces with a staple of about 155 mm and a mean diameter near 21 microns, against about 120 mm and 25 microns for the kara type, whose individual fibers spanned roughly 10 to 150 microns. Medullation, not coat type alone, drives handle: a Peruvian study found medullated fibers in similar proportions (around 46 to 47 percent by its classification) in both types. Commercial yarn is therefore graded by measured micron and dehairing quality rather than animal type.
llama.fabrics: Dehaired llama undercoat is spun into knitting yarns, often blended with wool or alpaca, and woven into blankets, throws and scarves. Natural colors (white, fawn, brown, grey and black) are frequently sold undyed. The coarse guard hair, which is unsuitable for next-to-skin wear, goes into rugs, saddle blankets, braided rope and cordage, uses with long Andean precedent. Woolly ch'aku fleece is also hand spun in highland communities for local textiles. Because much llama yarn comes from small herds, lots vary in grist and color from batch to batch.
llama.quality: Ask for a measured mean fiber diameter and, ideally, a medullation or comfort-factor figure; fine dehaired llama undercoat sits in the low 20s of microns, while unsorted fleece can be far coarser. Rub the fabric against the inside of your wrist: stiff, straight hairs standing out of the surface signal poor dehairing and will prickle. Terms such as baby llama are not defined in US or EU fiber-labeling law, so they do not substitute for a micron value. Llama and alpaca are hard to tell apart by eye, and cheap llama may be blended with wool or acrylic, so read the percentage label carefully.
pros: Well-dehaired undercoat gives warm, lofty yarn without the lanolin content of sheep wool.
A wide range of natural colors lets makers sell undyed yarn.
The coarse fraction has practical uses in rugs and rope, so less of the fleece is wasted.
Fiber is shorn from living animals that are also kept for pack work and meat.
cons: Guard hair left in the yarn causes prickle and visible stray hairs.
Fineness and medullation vary widely between animals, so quality is inconsistent between suppliers.
Heavily medullated fibers can dye unevenly and feel stiffer.
Supply is small and fragmented, which makes provenance hard to verify.
llama.impact: Llamas are raised mainly by smallholder and pastoral households in the Andes of Peru, Bolivia and Argentina, often on high grassland unsuitable for crops, and fiber is only one of several products alongside transport and meat. Camelids are often described as gentler on pasture than hard-hoofed livestock because of their padded feet, but no product life cycle assessment for llama yarn was found in this review, so claims of a lower footprint than sheep wool are unquantified. Shearing is annual or less frequent. Processing impacts resemble other specialty hair fibers: scouring water, energy for dehairing, and dyeing when fiber is not left natural. Fair payment to herders is a social question buyers can only check through supplier documentation.
llama.care: Hand wash in cool to lukewarm water (about 30 C or below) with a pH-neutral wool or hair detergent, keeping temperature constant to avoid felting. Do not wring; press out water, roll in a towel and dry flat away from direct heat and sunlight. Machine washing is only safe on a true wool cycle when the label permits it. Steam or iron on a low wool setting through a pressing cloth. Remove pills with a comb or fabric shaver. Store clean and dry with cedar or lavender as a deterrent, and inspect for clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae in spring and autumn. Chlorine bleach and alkaline detergents damage the keratin. The product label governs.
faq: It depends on processing. Dehaired llama undercoat in the low 20s of microns is soft enough for scarves and many sweaters. Itch comes from residual guard hairs and coarse fibers above about 30 microns, so poorly dehaired llama yarn can prickle while a well-sorted one does not.
What is the difference between llama and alpaca fiber?

Both are South American camelid fibers. Llamas descend from the guanaco and have historically been bred more for pack work, so their fleece averages coarser, with more guard hair and medullation. Alpaca has been selected for fiber. A fine, dehaired llama yarn can overlap with alpaca in feel.

Camelid fleece carries little of the wool grease that sheep produce, which is why llama is often suggested for people who react to lanolin. Sensitivity to the keratin itself, to dyes or to finishing chemicals is still possible, so test a small item first.

Only if the label says so. Untreated llama is a keratin fiber that can felt with heat, agitation and sudden temperature changes. Hand washing in cool water with a wool detergent and drying flat is the safe default.
notable: In a Bolivian study, woolly th'ampulli llamas averaged about 21 microns, close to many commercial alpaca grades.
Andean llama types are often named by herders' terms, ccara (with little wool) and ch'aku (woolly), rather than formal breed registries.
A Peruvian study found similar overall medullation in both llama fleece types, showing that coat type alone does not predict yarn softness.
